title: Revitalizing Transport: A Safer, Smarter Future for Baltimore's Network

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF pages 1-25 are the counted solution, including the summary, contents, memo, and references; PDF page 26 is the AI Use Report and is labeled Page 26 of 25 because it is excluded from the official 25-page solution limit.

context_sources.use: Complete official Problem D statement, requirements, supplied-data descriptions, glossary, and references.

limitations: All 26 physical pages and all five official problem pages were rendered and visually reviewed.
PDF pages 2, 8, 9, 14, and 19 are image- or equation-dominant and have sparse extracted text; page-aware renders were used to reconstruct their roles.
Many mathematical symbols are garbled in extracted text, so formulas were interpreted from page images, definitions, pseudocode, and surrounding prose; exact symbol-level reproduction remains unsafe.
A recurring diagonal and footer watermark obscures portions of text and figures and is not part of the team's analytical content.
The paper supplies no code, cleaned datasets, random seeds, optimization traces, machine-readable results, or complete data provenance needed to reproduce its numerical claims.
The official data files are described by COMAP, but the paper does not document precise versions, cleaning row counts, joins, exclusions, or generated artifacts.

official_requirements: Build one or more network models for a part or element of Baltimore's transportation system using the supplied vehicle-count data as relevant.
Analyze the impact of the Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse and/or reconstruction, including impacts on varied stakeholders.
Select a bus or pedestrian project and use the network model to assess its impact on varied stakeholders.
Recommend a transportation project that best improves residents' lives, including resident benefits, effects on other stakeholders, and disruptions to other transportation needs and lives.
Explain how the transportation system can best address safety.
Provide a one-page memo to the mayor describing two projects with benefits and drawbacks for people and safety.
Stay within the 25-page solution limit, with any AI Use Report outside that count.
task_reconstruction.paper_approach: Construct a Baltimore graph from supplied nodes and edges, delete Key Bridge edges for a collapse counterfactual, estimate congestion with a queueing model, estimate stakeholder accessibility with an A*-GA hybrid, place five bus stops by greedy coverage optimization and Monte Carlo area estimation, score community road availability, propose a highway-direction and exit redesign using an ADP-labeled formulation, and present a four-module safety software concept plus a mayoral memo.
task_reconstruction.paper_coverage: All explicit deliverable families appear: bridge analysis, bus project, resident-centered network project, stakeholder discussion, safety concept, memo, references, and AI disclosure.
coverage_gaps: Pedestrian infrastructure is not modeled, which is allowed because the official task permits a bus or pedestrian project.
Bridge reconstruction alternatives are not compared; the analysis focuses on edge deletion for collapse.
Stakeholder impacts are simulated through selected accessibility and radar scores without empirical welfare calibration or distributional analysis.
Safety is handled mainly through a software concept rather than a validated safety model tied to crash or hazard data.
Project disruptions, costs, feasibility, displacement, and implementation are mostly narrative rather than quantified.
No observed post-collapse holdout or external validation closes the model-to-recommendation chain.

section_map.summary: Organizes results by the three tasks, reports bus coverage rising from 61.37% to 78.13%, and names the bridge, transit, community, software, and sensitivity components.
Lists introduction, assumptions, data, bridge impact, transit optimization, community optimization, safety application, sensitivity, evaluation, and references.
Frames Baltimore's infrastructure challenge and restates bridge, bus or walking, and resident-centered recommendation tasks.
Displays a task-aligned workflow and begins assumptions about stakeholder flows, stable traffic, and vehicle arrivals.
Completes queueing assumptions, lists notation, names supplied files, applies geographic filtering, and drops selected fields.
Represents intersections and turning points as nodes, paths as edges, and shows an abstract Baltimore transportation network.
Maps graph nodes to coordinates and divides bridge-collapse impact into common congestion and stakeholder-specific accessibility.
Defines an M/M/c-style road queue using arrivals, road class speed, length, lane count, and AADT-derived traffic.
Introduces distinct accessibility pairings for residents, businesses, suburban residents, and other stakeholder groups.
Completes commuter, transit passenger, visitor, and entrepreneur accessibility definitions and begins the hybrid route search.
Defines Haversine distance, fitness and selection, provides hybrid pseudocode, and starts bridge-edge identification.
Deletes verified bridge-related edges and presents before-after topology and congestion plots.
Shows route simulation and stakeholder impact radar results and concludes the closure has severe effects.
Maps bus stops and routes, combines degree and betweenness centrality, and selects a sparse triangular area near the bridge.
Defines station service radius, new-stop locations, and a single objective maximizing covered land-area ratio.
Estimates circular coverage using 100,000 uniform geographic points and imposes station-count, region, and spacing constraints.
Uses a greedy method to place five stops at listed coordinates and displays Monte Carlo before-after coverage.
Simulates selected stakeholder trips and presents radar charts claimed to demonstrate improved convenience.
Combines connectivity, congestion, and land-use mixing into a community road-availability score.
Sets a direction-change objective and constraints and introduces an approximate-dynamic-programming formulation.
Selects a low-score area, proposes changing a highway direction and adding an exit, and shows before-after maps.
Narrates resident, entrepreneur, traveler, and congestion effects and introduces a safety software concept.
Shows four software modules and varies bus-stop service radius from 100 to 600 meters.
Identifies a coverage plateau, selects a radius by a qualitative tradeoff, asserts strengths, notes ADP runtime, and lists references.
Summarizes bridge reconstruction and bus-station projects, benefits, drawbacks, monitoring, and the safety software concept.
Discloses one Bing AI query about selecting a bus or sidewalk project and includes the returned generic planning steps.

contributions.summary: Creates a visually clear task-to-model decomposition that exposes the intended dependency between data, analysis, recommendations, safety, and communication.
Separates common network congestion from group-specific accessibility rather than treating all travelers identically.
Implements bridge collapse as an explicit graph-edge deletion, making the topology intervention auditable at a conceptual level.
Communicates topology, congestion, routes, accessibility, and stakeholder impacts through coordinated before-after views.
Provides exact coordinates for five recommended bus stops and a concrete before-after coverage estimate.
Combines access, congestion, and land-use context to target a neighborhood project rather than optimizing only global network efficiency.
Acknowledges that the highway redesign can help logistics while disrupting other intersections and nearby communities.
Meets the required mayoral memo format and communicates two projects, benefits, drawbacks, and monitoring in one page.

nodes.label: Official Baltimore stakeholder and safety requirements
OSM-derived nodes and edges, bus routes and stops, AADT
Bus coverage and greedy stop placement
Community road-availability index and ADP-labeled redesign

weak_links: Demand and stakeholder origins and destinations are assumed rather than calibrated.
Observed traffic counts are not connected to a validated network assignment.
Stakeholder scores and project effects are not empirically validated.
ADP mechanics and safety software operations are incomplete.
Costs, feasibility, uncertainty, and implementation are not propagated into recommendations.

assumptions.summary: Assumes stakeholder origins and destinations follow stable spatial patterns despite no reported trip-data calibration.
Excludes weather, incidents, and short-term disruptions to isolate the large bridge event.
Assumes independent random arrivals and nearly identical segment travel times to support queueing formulas.
Treats road-class speed, AADT conversion, lane count, and service time as adequate congestion inputs without reporting distributional diagnostics.
Treats every identified bridge edge as impassable and the remaining graph as the collapse counterfactual.
Treats 100,000 uniformly generated coordinates inside a bounding region as people needing bus service.
Assigns transition and reward behavior for a redesign without a reported empirical estimation process.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses nodes_all, edges_all, bus routes, bus stops, and AADT-style traffic inputs supplied with the official problem.
Restricts records by a stated latitude-longitude bounding box for Baltimore.
Drops selected sparse or unsuitable fields but does not provide row counts, missingness tables, or a transformation log.
Uses intersections and turning points as nodes and transportation paths as edges, with edge width interpreted as road importance.
Joins node identifiers to geographic coordinates to place the abstract graph on a map.
Uses I-695 reference codes and OSM identifiers to isolate and delete bridge segments.
Builds a stop-route network and scores nodes with degree and betweenness centrality.
Provides only five general references and omits a paper-level data dictionary, code, hashes, versions, seeds, and output tables.

models.summary: Represents Baltimore transportation elements as a geographic graph.
Uses an M/M/c-style queue with AADT-derived arrivals, lane servers, road speeds, and segment service time.
Maps stakeholder needs to accessibility between selected origin and destination classes.
Uses A* to seed a genetic path search with Haversine heuristics, inverse weights, crossover, mutation, and 100 generations.
Deletes bridge-related graph edges and recomputes outcomes.
Combines degree and betweenness centrality to diagnose the transit network and select an optimization area.
Maximizes the ratio of fixed-radius station coverage area to city area under count, region, and spacing constraints.
Uses uniform Monte Carlo points to estimate coverage for candidate stop locations.
Combines connectivity, congestion, and land-use mixing to score community access.
Introduces actions, transitions, rewards, and constraints for changing highway direction and adding an exit, but lacks a reproducible ADP algorithm.

verification.summary: Shows before-after network maps after bridge edge deletion but does not validate against observed post-collapse connectivity or flows.
Plots simulated changes across time and stakeholders without exact uncertainty intervals or observed holdouts.
Reports before-after coverage and coordinates but no random seed, convergence error, replication, or alternative optimizer baseline.
Uses polygon comparison as evidence of benefit without an empirical score definition or direction audit.
Shows a redesign before and after but provides no buildability, cost, demand-response, or held-out validation.
Varies only the bus service radius and observes a coverage plateau, leaving other model and decision uncertainties untested.
Claims authenticity and global optimality without certificates, benchmark gaps, observed comparisons, or reproducible artifacts.
Acknowledges high ADP time complexity but omits more consequential identification, calibration, feasibility, and uncertainty limitations.

results_trace.summary: Deleting bridge edges changes connectivity and shifts modeled congestion and routes; magnitude and observed validity remain unresolved.
Accessibility and radar outputs indicate simulated stakeholder effects, but score units, direction, sampling, and uncertainty are incomplete.
Five coordinates are recommended by a greedy coverage search.
Uniform-area service coverage is reported to increase from 61.37% to 78.13%.
Radar plots are interpreted as improved stakeholder travel convenience, but the plotted containment and score semantics are ambiguous.
Changing highway direction and adding an exit are claimed to improve road availability in a selected low-score area.
Benefits for residents and logistics are accompanied by narrative warnings about new congestion and nearby disruption.
Four interface modules are proposed, but no deployed or evaluated safety outcome is demonstrated.

writing_logic.summary: A task-by-task summary names methods and outputs and includes one headline quantitative change.
A single workflow figure previews the complete paper and provides strong navigation.
Moves from common congestion to individual stakeholder access, a clear global-to-local reasoning pattern.
Diagnoses the bus network, identifies an area, defines an objective, solves it, and returns to stakeholder effects.
Defines a targeting score before presenting intervention mechanics and results.
Separates strengths and weaknesses, but the stated weaknesses are narrower than the evidence limitations.
Compresses two projects into action, benefit, drawback, monitoring, and safety paragraphs for a municipal decision maker.

language_observations.summary: Uses compact task labels and exact percentages effectively, but overuses 'prove' for simulated and weakly validated results.
Restates the official task concisely while dropping some explicit safety, disruption, and memo detail that later sections must restore.
Names stakeholder groups directly and explains the practical meaning of accessibility for each group.
Pairs listed coordinates with a before-after percentage, improving actionability relative to figures alone.
Uses global-optimum and authenticity language beyond the supplied algorithmic and empirical evidence.
Maintains a decision-oriented tone but lacks quantified costs, uncertainty, implementation ownership, and trigger thresholds.

visualization_observations.summary: A dense but task-aligned diagram previews models, results, and communication artifacts.
Shows broad graph structure and road categories, but edge width semantics and legend details are not sufficiently auditable.
Side-by-side topology and a congestion line chart make the counterfactual easy to scan but omit exact effect tables and uncertainty.
Links route changes to stakeholder scores, but radar orientation and scoring basis are unclear.
Combines a city-scale graph and local map to motivate a target area, though demand and equity layers are absent.
Displays spatial sample density and lists exact coordinates, but no sampling error or baseline alternatives.
Uses repeated radar charts for groups, but polygon containment can mislead without score direction, common scales, and exact values.
Before-after aerial panels communicate the local construction concept but not engineering feasibility or quantified impacts.
The monotone plateau is visible and interfaces are polished, but neither substitutes for uncertainty analysis or operational validation.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: C: Clear task routing, extensive localized mapping, and visible deliverable coverage may have improved scanability, but the paper alone cannot establish why judges awarded it.
C: Supplying the requested municipal memo with two named projects and tradeoffs may have supported requirement completeness, but no judge rationale is present.

weaknesses.summary: No reproducible cleaning ledger, row counts, missingness report, dataset versions, or code.
Travel demand, stationarity, Poisson arrivals, independence, and common service times are asserted without calibration.
Road importance, weight, congestion, and travel time are described too loosely to establish coherent edge semantics.
AADT conversion, temporal profiles, capacity, queue interactions, and validation against segment counts are incomplete.
Stakeholder origins, destinations, weights, modes, time periods, and within-group distributions are not empirically grounded.
Hybrid path feasibility, population mechanics, mutation validity, convergence, compute budget, and comparison with standard shortest path are missing.
Edge deletion does not model rerouted demand, capacity spillovers, reconstruction alternatives, or observed post-collapse traffic.
Severity is asserted from plots without exact effect sizes, uncertainty, observed holdouts, or score orientation.
Centrality and visual sparsity are used as proxies for transit need without population, ridership, access-gap, or equity validation.
Uniform straight-line circular area coverage ignores population, demand, pedestrian networks, barriers, frequency, capacity, and reliability.
Five coordinates lack street-level feasibility, cost, construction, operations, repeated seeds, Monte Carlo error, and algorithm baselines.
Radar scores are self-constructed and ambiguous; the plotted containment may contradict the narrative without clear direction.
Composite orientation, normalization, weights, spatial resolution, and stakeholder validation are incomplete.
The method lacks a complete state, approximation architecture, training process, policy update, convergence evidence, and baseline.
The design is not supported by engineering feasibility, budget, demand response, displacement, safety, or uncertainty analysis.
Mockups do not specify live data, alert performance, privacy, accessibility, governance, responder ownership, or field validation.
Only service radius is varied, leaving structural, demand, parameter, algorithm, stakeholder, and project uncertainty untouched.
A coverage-curve midpoint is called a cost-walking balance although cost and walking disutility are absent from the objective.
Global-optimum, authenticity, effectiveness, proof, and robustness claims exceed the validation evidence.
Five general references do not support the numerous data, parameter, algorithm, simulation, and policy claims.
The memo omits exact costs, uncertainty, ownership, schedule, decision triggers, and measurable safety outcomes.

independent_extensions.summary: Build a time-dependent directed multigraph with calibrated origin-destination demand, capacity, observed counts, bridge closure and reconstruction scenarios, and distributional travel-time outputs.
Replace generic stakeholder radar scores with group-specific generalized cost, reliability, access, safety, and equity distributions.
Benchmark ordinary shortest path, k-shortest paths, traffic assignment, and the A*-GA hybrid under the same graph, cost definition, compute budget, and seeds.
Optimize bus stops on a pedestrian network using population, ridership, need, transfers, frequency, capital and operating costs, accessibility, and equity.
Reformulate community redesign as a multiobjective project portfolio with engineering feasibility, construction cost, displacement, induced demand, safety, emissions, and stakeholder tradeoffs.
If sequential redesign is required, implement a reproducible ADP or simulation-optimization policy with explicit state, dynamics, approximation, convergence, and held-out scenarios.
Turn the safety mockup into a requirements and evaluation specification covering data latency, alert errors, privacy, accessibility, emergency ownership, staged rollout, and measured outcomes.
Run joint global sensitivity over demand, capacities, service times, bridge scenarios, coverage radius, costs, stakeholder weights, and algorithm seeds, then report decision stability.
Publish a reproduction bundle with cleaned graph tables, transformations, code, seeds, exact result tables, figure data, and one-command regeneration.

candidate_rule_impacts.rationale: Require coherent network semantics, demand assignment, counterfactual design, calibration, and reproducibility for closure claims.
Operationalize stakeholder needs, distributions, equity, and tradeoffs beyond invented accessibility scores.
Replace unweighted circular area coverage with walk-network, demand, service, cost, feasibility, and equity measures.
Prevent an incomplete static redesign formulation from being treated as validated approximate dynamic programming.
Convert interface mockups into an operational safety-system specification and validation contract.

unresolved_questions: Which exact rows, fields, cleaning operations, graph direction rules, and edge-weight semantics produced the network?
How were AADT values converted into time-specific arrivals, and were queue assumptions tested against observed Baltimore counts?
What origins, destinations, modes, time periods, sample sizes, and score functions were used for each stakeholder?
Does the A*-GA procedure always produce connected feasible paths, and how does it compare with standard shortest-path and assignment methods?
Were the reported 61.37% and 78.13% coverage values stable across random seeds, and do they reflect population or only land area?
Why does the transit radar discussion say the before polygon surrounds the after polygon while claiming improvement, and which direction is favorable?
What exact state, approximation, training data, policy-update algorithm, and convergence criterion define the claimed ADP method?
What construction, operation, displacement, induced-demand, accessibility, and safety evidence supports the highway-direction and exit project?
Is the safety software implemented or only conceptual, and what data, alert accuracy, governance, and field evidence would support it?
